screens.title: SD-WAN Overlay Design and Transport Options
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build a mental model of the SD‑WAN overlay and why Transport Locators, System IPs, and Site IDs matter. The overlay is the logical fabric that rides on top of your existing underlay connections; it depends on correctly identifying each WAN interface and mapping it into the fabric using a TLOC. A TLOC is more than an address: it combines the transport IP, a descriptive color, and an encapsulation type so the controller and edge routers can negotiate secure tunnels and choose paths intelligently. We'll also connect this idea to common transport choices you already know: MPLS for predictable performance, broadband internet for cost savings, and LTE for rapid deployment or backup. Understanding these pieces prevents configuration errors that break tunnels, and it lets you design redundancy and policy that match application needs. For example, assigning the MPLS color to a broadband interface will mislead the controller and likely prevent tunnels from forming. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to map physical interfaces to logical TLOCs, choose appropriate colors and encapsulation, and reason about transport selection for availability and cost. Think about one branch you manage: which link would you label "mpls" and which one "biz-internet," and why?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and configure Transport Locators, assign appropriate TLOC colors and encapsulation types, and use System IPs and Site IDs to anchor devices within the fabric. You will also be able to differentiate transport types — MPLS, Internet, and LTE — and reason about when each is appropriate for performance, cost, and redundancy. Practically, you will map physical WAN interfaces to logical TLOCs and verify tunnel establishment using the provided show commands. These skills matter because incorrect mappings or duplicated identifiers break overlay routes, cause misapplied policies, and defeat the resilience benefits of SD‑WAN. For example, assigning the wrong TLOC color causes vSmart to advertise an interface as a transport it is not, which prevents tunnels from forming across the intended underlay path. Each objective pairs a configuration skill with a verification habit, so you not only change settings but also confirm underlay reachability and OMP TLOC advertisement. This chapter combines conceptual understanding with CLI-focused practice so you leave with both a mental model and actionable commands.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Verification
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on hands‑on outcomes: configuring TLOC extensions, setting System IP and Site ID, and verifying overlay health. You'll practice a CLI workflow to set two transport interfaces, apply tunnel encapsulation, and ensure vSmart advertises the TLOCs. The verification habit includes checking underlay reachability first, then confirming OMP TLOC advertisement and control connections. Why this order? If the underlay cannot route the transport IPs, TLOCs never appear and tunnels will not form. A helpful mental checklist: underlay IPs should ping, System IP must be unique and configured, Site IDs must be assigned per physical site, and TLOC colors should reflect the real transport. Missteps to avoid include duplicated Site IDs across distinct locations or mislabeling colors — both lead to incorrect policy targeting or failed negotiation. By the end you'll be able to run show sdwan omp tlocs and interpret the output to confirm which TLOCs are available for tunnel pairing. Think of verification as the final safety check that proves your overlay will behave as intended under normal and failover conditions.

screens.title: What is a TLOC?
screens.narratorSegment: A Transport Locator or TLOC is the fundamental unit that identifies a WAN interface in Cisco SD‑WAN. It is not merely a single IP address; it is a three‑part identifier composed of the transport IP, a TLOC color, and the encapsulation type. The transport IP is the actual address reachable in the underlay. The color is a descriptive label like mpls or biz‑internet that tells vSmart the kind of transport and how to apply policy. The encapsulation indicates whether IPsec or GRE will be used to secure the data plane traffic for that TLOC. Together these attributes let vSmart and edge routers advertise available transports and negotiate which TLOCs form tunnels to one another. A concrete example: a branch router with an MPLS interface that has IP 10.0.1.1 would present a TLOC whose transport IP is 10.0.1.1, whose color is mpls, and whose encapsulation is ipsec. A common misconception is thinking the TLOC is only the transport IP. That leads to errors when you rely on IP alone for policy decisions. The core takeaway is that the overlay treats the TLOC as the transport identity — policies, path preferences, and tunnel pairing rely on all three attributes. Ask yourself: do the IP, color, and encapsulation accurately describe the physical link you intend to use?

content.html:
Core Concept

What is a TLOC?

A TLOC is the overlay identity for a WAN interface, composed of a transport IP, a TLOC color, and an encapsulation type.

Transport IP
The underlay address that must be reachable before an overlay tunnel can form.
TLOC color
A label such as mpls or biz-internet used for policy and path selection.
Encapsulation
IPsec (recommended) or GRE determines how data plane traffic is carried securely over the underlay.
Example
TLOC:
 transport-ip: 10.0.1.1
 color: mpls
 encapsulation: ipsec
Misconception to avoid: treating the transport IP as the only identifier. If the color is wrong, vSmart will advertise an incorrect transport type and tunnels may not form as expected.
Key Takeaway

Always define TLOCs with a correct transport IP, meaningful color, and the intended encapsulation so the overlay behaves predictably.

screens.title: TLOC Color: labeling transports for policy
screens.narratorSegment: TLOC color is a descriptive label that tells the SD‑WAN controller how to treat a transport. It is intentionally human-readable: examples include mpls, biz-internet, public-internet, and lte. You assign a color to each TLOC so vSmart can categorize available transports and apply centralized policies accordingly. For example, you might prefer sending critical application traffic over TLOCs labeled mpls because those links typically offer SLAs and QoS, while bulk traffic could use biz‑internet. The process of using colors for policy follows a few steps: first ensure each physical interface is reachable in the underlay; then assign a color that reflects the transport characteristics; next advertise the TLOC so vSmart knows which colors exist on each site; finally create policies that match color names for path selection or failover. A common mistake is assigning the same color across different transport types or mislabeling an internet link as mpls. That breaks the intended policy model because vSmart and peers will assume a transport capability that doesn't exist. Always document color conventions and apply them consistently across templates and CLI configurations. Which color will you pick for a low-latency MPLS circuit and why?

keyIdea.title: Color guides policy
keyIdea.text: TLOC colors categorize transports for vSmart so centralized policies can prioritize or redirect traffic based on transport characteristics.

content.html:
Process Flow

Assigning and using TLOC colors

1
Verify underlay reachability
Ping transport IPs and confirm routing before advertising TLOCs.
2
Assign a meaningful color
Choose a color name that maps to the transport characteristics you expect.
3
Advertise the TLOC
vSmart learns colors and available TLOCs via OMP and uses them for policy decisions.
4
Create color-based policies
Match colors in policies to prefer, block, or failover between transports.
Comparison: color examples
mpls
Used for predictable SLA-backed circuits; prefer for critical apps.
biz-internet / public-internet
Broadband transport for general traffic or failover.
lte
Wireless backup or temporary connectivity; higher cost per GB but quick deployment.
Common mistake

Mislabeling an Internet link as mpls causes vSmart to advertise the wrong transport type, leading peers to attempt tunnels over an incompatible underlay path.

screens.title: Encapsulation: IPsec vs GRE
screens.narratorSegment: Encapsulation determines how data plane traffic is carried over the underlay and what protections are applied. In modern Cisco SD‑WAN, IPsec is the default and recommended encapsulation because it provides encryption and authentication, protecting data in transit and preventing tampering. GRE is supported in specific scenarios, typically for integration with legacy or non‑SD‑WAN devices where IPsec termination is not feasible. A practical example: use IPsec when you need confidentiality and integrity between two branch routers. Use GRE when you must interoperate with an older router that cannot terminate IPsec or when a cleartext tunnel is acceptable for specific legacy protocols. A common misconception is that GRE is simply "faster" because it lacks encryption; in reality, GRE removes confidentiality but does not inherently improve application performance and can expose traffic to inspection or manipulation. When designing the overlay, prefer IPsec unless you have a compelling operational requirement for GRE and have accounted for its security limitations. The design choice affects policy and compliance, so document which TLOCs will use IPsec and which rare cases will use GRE. Encapsulation: IPsec vs GRE means ipsec secures the data plane and is preferred; gre is for special integration scenarios but lacks default encryption.. In practical terms, security and use cases for data plane tunnels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison

IPsec vs GRE

IPsec
Provides encryption and authentication. Use for secure site-to-site tunnels and compliance-sensitive traffic.
GRE
Used for integration with legacy devices or scenarios where IPsec termination is not possible. Lacks built-in encryption by default.
Scenario
A data center connecting to a branch carrying regulated traffic should use IPsec encapsulation for compliance. A temporary lab link connecting to a legacy router may use GRE if IPsec termination is not supported on the legacy device.
Misconception

Choosing GRE to "speed things up" ignores the security and policy implications; lack of encryption exposes traffic and may violate requirements.

Key Takeaway

Prefer IPsec for the data plane unless you have a documented interoperability need for GRE and appropriate compensating controls.

screens.title: System IP and Site ID
screens.narratorSegment: System IP and Site ID are persistent identifiers used by the SD‑WAN control plane. The System IP is a loopback address assigned to each vEdge or cEdge router. It acts like a router ID: vSmart uses the System IP to uniquely identify a device even when physical interface IPs change. Site ID, on the other hand, is a numerical label assigned to a physical location such as a branch or data center. All routers in the same physical site share the same Site ID so the controller can apply site-level policy and understand topology. For example, if two routers are co‑located in Branch_A, both would use Site ID 100, while routers in the datacenter might use 200. A common misstep is assigning the same Site ID to geographically distinct sites; that causes vSmart to treat them as one location and can result in wrong policy application or route advertisements. Another practical point: ensure System IPs are unique across the entire fabric; duplicate System IPs confuse the control plane. When you configure devices, think of System IP as the router's persistent name and Site ID as the building it belongs to. This mental separation helps prevent misconfiguration during template deployment or CLI edits.

keyIdea.title: Stable identifiers
keyIdea.text: System IP uniquely names a router; Site ID groups routers by physical site. Both must be unique and consistent to avoid topology errors.

content.html:
Definition

System IP

A persistent loopback address assigned to each router to serve as its identifier in the overlay.

Example: system-ip 172.16.10.1 — this stays constant even if physical interfaces change, so vSmart can always identify the device.
Definition

Site ID

A numerical identifier assigned to a physical or logical location; all devices at the same site share this ID.

Example: site-id 10 for Branch_A; site-id 200 for DataCenter_B. Use unique numbers per location.
Common mistake

Assigning the same Site ID to different physical sites results in incorrect topology and policy application. Always map Site IDs to actual locations and keep System IPs unique.

screens.title: Transport Options: MPLS, Internet, LTE
screens.narratorSegment: Transport options determine the underlay characteristics available to your SD‑WAN overlay. The most common transports are MPLS, Internet (broadband/DIA), and LTE or 5G. MPLS is typically the "private" option with predictable performance and QoS capabilities, making it ideal for business‑critical applications. Internet links are cost effective and ubiquitous but have variable performance and should be used for non-critical traffic or as a secondary path. LTE and 5G are best used for rapid deployment, backup paths, or remote or mobile sites. In practice, a resilient design often combines transports: the primary path might be MPLS with a broadband internet connection for failover and an LTE backup for last‑mile redundancy. When you assign TLOC colors, reflect these choices: color mpls for the MPLS link, biz‑internet for business broadband, and lte for the cellular path. This labeling allows vSmart to implement policies that prefer MPLS for latency- and jitter‑sensitive flows while using internet links for less critical traffic or to provide additional bandwidth. Consider cost per GB, SLA requirements, and deployment time when selecting which transports to deploy at each site. Which transport mix would you choose for a remote office with limited budget but critical VoIP needs?

keyIdea.text: MPLS offers SLA-backed performance; Internet gives cost savings and ubiquity; LTE provides fast deployment and backup. Use a mix for resilience.

content.html:
Architecture

Transport options

MPLS
Private backbone, predictable performance, preferred for critical applications; assign color mpls.
Internet (Broadband/DIA)
Cost effective and widely available; variable performance; use for general traffic or as secondary.
LTE / 5G
Quick deployment and backup option; higher cost per GB, useful for temporary or mobile sites.
Design pattern
Typical branch: primary MPLS for latency-sensitive apps, broadband for internet breakout or secondary transport, and LTE as a final failover. Label TLOCs accordingly and create policies that prefer the desired color.
Key Takeaway

Choose transports based on SLA and cost, and reflect those choices in TLOC colors so the controller can apply the right policy.

screens.title: Tunnel establishment and OMP advertisement
screens.narratorSegment: Tunnel establishment in Cisco SD‑WAN is orchestrated by the control plane and relies on a few sequential processes. First, each edge router authenticates with vBond and learns controller locations, establishing secure control connections to vManage and vSmart. The router then advertises its TLOCs via OMP to vSmart. vSmart aggregates all known TLOCs and advertises them to other routers so each edge knows which transports exist and what colors they carry. After learning TLOCs, edge routers can form direct IPsec tunnels to reachable TLOCs on other routers, creating the overlay data plane. For example, a branch with an mpls TLOC and a biz-internet TLOC will advertise both; another branch with a biz-internet TLOC can form an IPsec tunnel to the branch's biz-internet TLOC if the underlay permits reachability. A common misconception is that tunnels are formed automatically without validating underlay reachability; in reality, if the transport IPs cannot be reached at the underlay level, the IPsec negotiation cannot succeed. Verification steps include show sdwan omp tlocs to list advertised TLOCs, and show sdwan control connections to confirm control plane connectivity. Use these outputs to trace whether a missing tunnel is caused by control plane issues, absent TLOC advertisement, or underlay routing failures.

keyIdea.title: Control-plane choreography
keyIdea.text: vSmart learns TLOCs via OMP and informs edges so they can form IPsec tunnels; underlay reachability is required for data plane formation.

content.html:
Process Flow

How tunnels are established

  1. Edge authenticates with vBond and learns controllers.
  2. Edge establishes control connections to vSmart/vManage.
  3. Edge advertises its TLOCs via OMP to vSmart.
  4. vSmart distributes TLOCs to other edges.
  5. Edges form IPsec tunnels to reachable TLOCs based on policy and reachability.
Verification commands
show sdwan omp tlocs
show sdwan control connections
show sdwan omp routes
Key Takeaway

Control plane connectivity and accurate TLOC advertisement are prerequisites for IPsec tunnel formation; use show commands to pinpoint gaps.

screens.title: CLI: configuring TLOC extensions on a cEdge
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the CLI workflow to configure two transports on a cEdge and define TLOCs. The process begins by configuring the physical interfaces with the correct underlay IPs. Next you set the System IP and Site ID in the sdwan configuration so the router appears with a persistent identifier. Then, within VPN 0, you convert the interfaces into tunnel-interfaces and specify encapsulation and color. In modern IOS XE SD‑WAN the tunnel-interface command implicitly creates the TLOC. After applying these settings, verify underlay connectivity with pings to the transport IPs, then run show sdwan omp tlocs to confirm the TLOCs are advertised and show sdwan control connections to verify control channel health. A common error is skipping the underlay verification step and assuming the overlay will form. For example, configure GigabitEthernet0/1 with IP 10.0.1.1/24 and color mpls, and GigabitEthernet0/2 with IP 20.0.1.1/24 and color biz-internet. The provided CLI block shows the necessary commands. Core CLI

Configuration (example)

!

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting overlay issues begins with a small set of common mistakes that repeatedly cause failures. First, miscolored TLOCs: assigning the wrong color to an interface causes vSmart to advertise an incorrect transport type, which leads peers to expect a different underlay path and can prevent IPsec negotiation. Fix: correct the color to match the actual transport and re-advertise. Second, duplicated Site IDs across different physical sites cause vSmart to treat separate locations as one, misapplying site-scoped policies. Fix: ensure Site IDs are uniquely assigned per physical location and update templates or CLI accordingly. Third, underlay routing gaps: if transport IPs are not routable between devices, tunnels simply will not form. Fix: validate routing, BGP, or static routes in the underlay before expecting the overlay to work. When you investigate, maintain this sequence: verify underlay reachability with pings, inspect TLOC advertisement with show sdwan omp tlocs, then check control connections. Each verification step narrows the cause-to-effect chain. Keep a simple triage checklist and document corrective actions so future rollouts avoid the same missteps. Troubleshooting

Common mistakes and fixes

Miscolored TLOC
Symptoms: tunnels not forming to expected transport. Fix: update color to reflect actual transport and re-advertise.
Duplicate Site ID
Symptoms: incorrect site-level policy. Fix: assign unique Site IDs per physical site and update templates.
Underlay routing gap
Symptoms: transport IPs unreachable. Fix: correct underlay routing, BGP or static routes, then verify pings.
Triage order

Ping transport IPs → show sdwan omp tlocs → show sdwan control connections. This sequence narrows root cause quickly.

Safety note

Never change colors or Site IDs in production without documenting the change and understanding the policy impact; do it in templates for consistency.

screens.title: Multi-transport design: resilience and policy
screens.narratorSegment: A resilient SD‑WAN design leverages multiple transports to balance cost and availability. Consider a branch with an MPLS circuit and a broadband internet link. You create two TLOCs: one colored mpls for the MPLS interface and one colored biz‑internet for the broadband interface. Centralized policies on vSmart can prefer mpls for voice and ERP traffic while allowing bulk backups over biz‑internet. If MPLS fails, the policy can failover traffic to the biz‑internet TLOC. Adding an LTE TLOC provides a third path for last‑mile resilience; it can be configured as a secondary or emergency-only route. The overlay supports full or partial meshes of IPsec tunnels between sites depending on policy, which reduces backhaul and improves latency for inter-branch traffic. When designing, document which color is primary for each application class and ensure your templates assign colors consistently. A design pitfall is expecting identical behavior from different transport types; MPLS typically supports QoS and guaranteed latency while internet links do not, so treat them differently in SLAs and policy. The core design question: which transport will carry your critical application in normal and failure conditions, and are TLOCs labeled to make that intent explicit?

Multi-transport branch design

Secondary

screens.title: Policy implications of transport labeling
screens.narratorSegment: Transport labeling drives how policies steer traffic. When colors are assigned consistently, you can write vSmart policies that match those colors and implement expected behavior for application classes. For instance, a policy that matches color mpls can prefer that transport for voice, ensuring low latency and prioritization. Conversely, if colors are inconsistent between sites — for example, some sites using biz-internet and others using public-internet for similar broadband circuits — your policies may not match as intended, leading to unpredictable routing. Best practice is to define and document a color naming convention and enforce it through templates or automation. Also, consider naming for administrative clarity: reserve mpls for provider-backed circuits, biz-internet for managed broadband, public-internet for direct internet access, and lte for cellular backups. A common operational mistake is ad-hoc color assignment during emergency changes; this creates long-term policy drift. Instead, update templates and apply controlled changes that maintain naming consistency so that steering, SLA-based selection, and failover work reliably across the fabric. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a mental model of the SD‑WAN overlay and why Transport Locators, System IPs, and Site IDs matter. The overlay is the logical fabric that rides on top of your existing underlay connections; it depends on correctly identifying each WAN interface and mapping it into the fabric using a TLOC. A TLOC is more than an address: it combines the transport IP, a descriptive color, and an encapsulation type so the controller and edge routers can negotiate secure tunnels and choose paths intelligently. We'll also connect this idea to common transport choices you already know: MPLS for predictable performance, broadband internet for cost savings, and LTE for rapid deployment or backup. Understanding these pieces prevents configuration errors that break tunnels, and it lets you design redundancy and policy that match application needs. For example, assigning the MPLS color to a broadband interface will mislead the controller and likely prevent tunnels from forming. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to map physical interfaces to logical TLOCs, choose appropriate colors and encapsulation, and reason about transport selection for availability and cost. Think about one branch you manage: which link would you label "mpls" and which one "biz-internet," and why?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and configure Transport Locators, assign appropriate TLOC colors and encapsulation types, and use System IPs and Site IDs to anchor devices within the fabric. You will also be able to differentiate transport types — MPLS, Internet, and LTE — and reason about when each is appropriate for performance, cost, and redundancy. Practically, you will map physical WAN interfaces to logical TLOCs and verify tunnel establishment using the provided show commands. These skills matter because incorrect mappings or duplicated identifiers break overlay routes, cause misapplied policies, and defeat the resilience benefits of SD‑WAN. For example, assigning the wrong TLOC color causes vSmart to advertise an interface as a transport it is not, which prevents tunnels from forming across the intended underlay path. Each objective pairs a configuration skill with a verification habit, so you not only change settings but also confirm underlay reachability and OMP TLOC advertisement. This chapter combines conceptual understanding with CLI-focused practice so you leave with both a mental model and actionable commands.

This second objectives screen focuses on hands‑on outcomes: configuring TLOC extensions, setting System IP and Site ID, and verifying overlay health. You'll practice a CLI workflow to set two transport interfaces, apply tunnel encapsulation, and ensure vSmart advertises the TLOCs. The verification habit includes checking underlay reachability first, then confirming OMP TLOC advertisement and control connections. Why this order? If the underlay cannot route the transport IPs, TLOCs never appear and tunnels will not form. A helpful mental checklist: underlay IPs should ping, System IP must be unique and configured, Site IDs must be assigned per physical site, and TLOC colors should reflect the real transport. Missteps to avoid include duplicated Site IDs across distinct locations or mislabeling colors — both lead to incorrect policy targeting or failed negotiation. By the end you'll be able to run show sdwan omp tlocs and interpret the output to confirm which TLOCs are available for tunnel pairing. Think of verification as the final safety check that proves your overlay will behave as intended under normal and failover conditions.

A Transport Locator or TLOC is the fundamental unit that identifies a WAN interface in Cisco SD‑WAN. It is not merely a single IP address; it is a three‑part identifier composed of the transport IP, a TLOC color, and the encapsulation type. The transport IP is the actual address reachable in the underlay. The color is a descriptive label like mpls or biz‑internet that tells vSmart the kind of transport and how to apply policy. The encapsulation indicates whether IPsec or GRE will be used to secure the data plane traffic for that TLOC. Together these attributes let vSmart and edge routers advertise available transports and negotiate which TLOCs form tunnels to one another. A concrete example: a branch router with an MPLS interface that has IP 10.0.1.1 would present a TLOC whose transport IP is 10.0.1.1, whose color is mpls, and whose encapsulation is ipsec. A common misconception is thinking the TLOC is only the transport IP. That leads to errors when you rely on IP alone for policy decisions. The core takeaway is that the overlay treats the TLOC as the transport identity — policies, path preferences, and tunnel pairing rely on all three attributes. Ask yourself: do the IP, color, and encapsulation accurately describe the physical link you intend to use?

TLOC color is a descriptive label that tells the SD‑WAN controller how to treat a transport. It is intentionally human-readable: examples include mpls, biz-internet, public-internet, and lte. You assign a color to each TLOC so vSmart can categorize available transports and apply centralized policies accordingly. For example, you might prefer sending critical application traffic over TLOCs labeled mpls because those links typically offer SLAs and QoS, while bulk traffic could use biz‑internet. The process of using colors for policy follows a few steps: first ensure each physical interface is reachable in the underlay; then assign a color that reflects the transport characteristics; next advertise the TLOC so vSmart knows which colors exist on each site; finally create policies that match color names for path selection or failover. A common mistake is assigning the same color across different transport types or mislabeling an internet link as mpls. That breaks the intended policy model because vSmart and peers will assume a transport capability that doesn't exist. Always document color conventions and apply them consistently across templates and CLI configurations. Which color will you pick for a low-latency MPLS circuit and why?

Encapsulation determines how data plane traffic is carried over the underlay and what protections are applied. In modern Cisco SD‑WAN, IPsec is the default and recommended encapsulation because it provides encryption and authentication, protecting data in transit and preventing tampering. GRE is supported in specific scenarios, typically for integration with legacy or non‑SD‑WAN devices where IPsec termination is not feasible. A practical example: use IPsec when you need confidentiality and integrity between two branch routers. Use GRE when you must interoperate with an older router that cannot terminate IPsec or when a cleartext tunnel is acceptable for specific legacy protocols. A common misconception is that GRE is simply "faster" because it lacks encryption; in reality, GRE removes confidentiality but does not inherently improve application performance and can expose traffic to inspection or manipulation. When designing the overlay, prefer IPsec unless you have a compelling operational requirement for GRE and have accounted for its security limitations. The design choice affects policy and compliance, so document which TLOCs will use IPsec and which rare cases will use GRE. Encapsulation: IPsec vs GRE means ipsec secures the data plane and is preferred; gre is for special integration scenarios but lacks default encryption.. In practical terms, security and use cases for data plane tunnels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

System IP and Site ID are persistent identifiers used by the SD‑WAN control plane. The System IP is a loopback address assigned to each vEdge or cEdge router. It acts like a router ID: vSmart uses the System IP to uniquely identify a device even when physical interface IPs change. Site ID, on the other hand, is a numerical label assigned to a physical location such as a branch or data center. All routers in the same physical site share the same Site ID so the controller can apply site-level policy and understand topology. For example, if two routers are co‑located in Branch_A, both would use Site ID 100, while routers in the datacenter might use 200. A common misstep is assigning the same Site ID to geographically distinct sites; that causes vSmart to treat them as one location and can result in wrong policy application or route advertisements. Another practical point: ensure System IPs are unique across the entire fabric; duplicate System IPs confuse the control plane. When you configure devices, think of System IP as the router's persistent name and Site ID as the building it belongs to. This mental separation helps prevent misconfiguration during template deployment or CLI edits.

Transport options determine the underlay characteristics available to your SD‑WAN overlay. The most common transports are MPLS, Internet (broadband/DIA), and LTE or 5G. MPLS is typically the "private" option with predictable performance and QoS capabilities, making it ideal for business‑critical applications. Internet links are cost effective and ubiquitous but have variable performance and should be used for non-critical traffic or as a secondary path. LTE and 5G are best used for rapid deployment, backup paths, or remote or mobile sites. In practice, a resilient design often combines transports: the primary path might be MPLS with a broadband internet connection for failover and an LTE backup for last‑mile redundancy. When you assign TLOC colors, reflect these choices: color mpls for the MPLS link, biz‑internet for business broadband, and lte for the cellular path. Tunnel establishment in Cisco SD‑WAN is orchestrated by the control plane and relies on a few sequential processes. First, each edge router authenticates with vBond and learns controller locations, establishing secure control connections to vManage and vSmart. The router then advertises its TLOCs via OMP to vSmart. vSmart aggregates all known TLOCs and advertises them to other routers so each edge knows which transports exist and what colors they carry. After learning TLOCs, edge routers can form direct IPsec tunnels to reachable TLOCs on other routers, creating the overlay data plane. For example, a branch with an mpls TLOC and a biz-internet TLOC will advertise both; another branch with a biz-internet TLOC can form an IPsec tunnel to the branch's biz-internet TLOC if the underlay permits reachability. A common misconception is that tunnels are formed automatically without validating underlay reachability; in reality, if the transport IPs cannot be reached at the underlay level, the IPsec negotiation cannot succeed. Verification steps include show sdwan omp tlocs to list advertised TLOCs, and show sdwan control connections to confirm control plane connectivity. Use these outputs to trace whether a missing tunnel is caused by control plane issues, absent TLOC advertisement, or underlay routing failures.

Troubleshooting overlay issues begins with a small set of common mistakes that repeatedly cause failures. First, miscolored TLOCs: assigning the wrong color to an interface causes vSmart to advertise an incorrect transport type, which leads peers to expect a different underlay path and can prevent IPsec negotiation. Fix: correct the color to match the actual transport and re-advertise. Second, duplicated Site IDs across different physical sites cause vSmart to treat separate locations as one, misapplying site-scoped policies. Fix: ensure Site IDs are uniquely assigned per physical location and update templates or CLI accordingly. Third, underlay routing gaps: if transport IPs are not routable between devices, tunnels simply will not form. Fix: validate routing, BGP, or static routes in the underlay before expecting the overlay to work. When you investigate, maintain this sequence: verify underlay reachability with pings, inspect TLOC advertisement with show sdwan omp tlocs, then check control connections. Here are the essential concepts to remember from this chapter. First, a TLOC is a composite identifier of transport IP, TLOC color, and encapsulation: it is the overlay's address for a WAN interface and the basis for tunnel pairing. Second, TLOC color is a policy label — choose and apply colors consistently so vSmart can steer traffic according to your intent. Third, encapsulation matters: IPsec is the recommended default for secure data plane tunnels; GRE is for special integration use cases only. These three points form the core of overlay design and policy behavior. Keep a verification routine: validate underlay reachability first, then confirm TLOC advertisement with show sdwan omp tlocs and control plane health with show sdwan control connections. Finally, assign unique System IPs and Site IDs: System IP identifies each router persistently, and Site ID groups devices by physical location, driving correct policy application. With these pieces in place, your SD‑WAN fabric will form reliable tunnels and allow vSmart to apply application-aware, transport-aware policies.

Third, verify underlay routing before expecting overlay tunnels: use pings and the show sdwan commands to confirm TLOC advertisement and control-plane health.
